title: CAE Inc. Factum to Federal Court of Appeal (Mar 2022)
subject: A Below-Market Repayable Loan Cannot Be Split: Government Assistance in Full
summary: In CAE Inc. v. His Majesty the King, 2022 FCA 178, the Federal Court of Appeal rejected the bifurcation argument in CAE's factum and held that its below-market, unconditionally repayable SADI loan from Industry Canada was government assistance in full. For Canadian SR&ED claimants, a non-commercial loan cannot be split; the entire principal reduces qualified expenditures.
metaDescription: Read the March 2022 CAE Inc. Factum to the Canadian Federal Court of Appeal regarding SR&ED tax credits and government assistance.

body.text: 1. Executive Summary & Case Background

The appellate litigation in CAE Inc. v. His Majesty the King, 2022 FCA 178 (also indexed in French as CAE Inc. c. Canada, 2022 CAF 178, Docket A-264-21), affirming the Tax Court of Canada decision in CAE Inc. v. The Queen, 2021 TCC 57 (CAE Inc. c. La Reine, 2021 CCI 57, Docket 2016-4984(IT)G), represents a watershed moment in Canadian Scientific Research and Experimental Development (SR&ED / Recherche scientifique et développement expérimental, RS&DE) tax jurisprudence. Rather than turning on whether the taxpayer's underlying engineering activities satisfied the scientific eligibility criteria of subsection 248(1) of the Canadian Income Tax Act, R.S.C. 1985, c. 1 (5th Supp.) (the "ITA" or Loi de l'impôt sur le revenu, "LIR"), the dispute centered on the statutory disqualification of SR&ED expenditure pools and Investment Tax Credits ("ITCs" / crédits d'impôt à l'investissement, "CII") resulting from public-sector project financing. Specifically, the courts examined whether an unconditionally repayable, interest-bearing, full-recourse loan advanced by a federal government department on concessional (below-market) terms constituted "government assistance" (aide gouvernementale) in its entirety, thereby reducing both the taxpayer's deductible SR&ED expenditures and the qualified expenditures on which its SR&ED ITCs were computed; the Minister additionally included part of the 2012 loan proceeds in taxable business income under paragraph 12(1)(x), a question the Tax Court did not need to decide.
Factual Matrix and the Taxpayer's Claim

The appellant, CAE Inc. ("CAE"), is a premier Canadian aerospace and defence technology corporation headquartered in Montreal, Quebec, globally recognized for designing advanced flight simulators and integrated training systems. On March 30, 2009, CAE entered into a contribution agreement with the federal Minister of Industry (Department of Industry Canada / Industrie Canada, subsequently Innovation, Science and Economic Development Canada, "ISED") under the Strategic Aerospace and Defence Initiative ("SADI" / Initiative stratégique pour l'aérospatiale et la défense, "ISAD"). The SADI Agreement was executed to help finance "Project Falcon" (Projet Falcon), a multi-year SR&ED program undertaken by CAE to develop next-generation aerospace simulation technologies.

Under the terms of the SADI Agreement and its subsequent amendments, Industry Canada committed to providing financial contributions of up to $250,000,000 over a five-year research and development phase by reimbursing a fixed percentage of CAE's eligible Project Falcon SR&ED expenditures. CAE's appellate factum describes the arrangement as a $250 million loan (the "Capital") repayable in 15 fixed annual instalments due each July 31 from 2015 to 2029, totalling $337,500,000, or 1.35 times the amounts advanced. During the specific taxation years under appeal—the fiscal periods ended March 31, 2012, and March 31, 2013—CAE received or became entitled to receive SADI contributions of $57,084,395 and $59,148,888, respectively.

Critically, the SADI financial contributions were neither outright grants nor conditionally repayable royalty advances; they were structured as a non-forgivable, unconditionally repayable loan generating an implicit return of approximately 2.5% for the Department of Industry, repayable in 15 annual instalments beginning July 31, 2015, after the 2009–2014 contribution period. In filing its corporate T2 income tax returns and Form T661 (Scientific Research and Experimental Development (SR&ED) Expenditures Claim) for the 2012 and 2013 taxation years, CAE took the position that because it was unconditionally obligated to repay 100% of the principal borrowed under the SADI Agreement plus interest, the loan proceeds did not constitute "government assistance". Consequently, CAE did not deduct the $57,084,395 (2012) and $59,148,888 (2013) from its qualified SR&ED expenditure pools, claimed full SR&ED ITCs on the Project Falcon outlays, and excluded the loan principal from its taxable income.
The Tax Authority's Challenge

Following an audit of CAE's 2012 and 2013 taxation years, the Minister of National Revenue (administered by the Canada Revenue Agency, "CRA" / Agence du revenu du Canada, "ARC") issued reassessments recharacterizing the SADI Capital received or receivable in those years—$57,084,395 for 2012 and $59,148,888 for 2013—as "government assistance". The Minister's challenge rested on the premise that the SADI Agreement was not an "ordinary commercial agreement" (entente commerciale ordinaire). Because the implicit 2.5% rate of return was significantly below the market rate for a comparable loan, the CRA asserted that the entire capital principal of the loan fell within the statutory ambit of "any other form of assistance". This reassessment triggered a punitive double fiscal impact: first, it reduced CAE's deductible SR&ED expenditures under paragraph 37(1)(d) by $41,003,491 (2012) and $40,652,951 (2013) and reduced its qualified expenditures for ITC purposes under subsection 127(18) by $57,084,395 (2012) and $59,148,888 (2013); second, under subparagraphs 12(1)(x)(iv) and (v), the CRA added $14,806,939 to CAE's 2012 income, being the excess of the amount received or receivable in 2012 ($55,810,430) over CAE's SR&ED expenditures for that year ($41,003,491).
Governing Statutory Framework in Canada

The dispute in CAE Inc. is governed by four interlocking mechanisms of the federal Income Tax Act (Canada) that regulate the tax treatment of public funding for research and development. At the foundation of this regime is subsection 127(9) of the ITA, which defines "government assistance" (aide gouvernementale) exhaustively yet expansively as assistance from a government, municipality, or other public authority whether as a grant, subsidy, forgivable loan, deduction from tax, investment allowance, or as "any other form of assistance" (toute autre forme d'aide), excluding only a deduction under subsection 127(5) or (6).

This foundational definition directly feeds into the expenditure pool and tax credit clawback rules under paragraph 37(1)(d) and subsection 127(18) of the ITA. Paragraph 37(1)(d) mandates that a taxpayer's cumulative pool of deductible SR&ED expenditures carried on in Canada is reduced by the amount of any government assistance, non-government assistance, or contract payment that the taxpayer has received, is entitled to receive, or can reasonably be expected to receive in respect of SR&ED. Operating in parallel, subsection 127(18) reduces a taxpayer's "qualified expenditures" (dépenses admissibles) for the purpose of computing SR&ED Investment Tax Credits by any government or non-government assistance received, receivable, or reasonably expected to be received at the filing deadline for the taxation year.

Where government assistance exceeds the available SR&ED expenditure pool deductions or is not otherwise applied to reduce the cost of depreciable property or deductible outlays, subparagraph 12(1)(x)(iv) of the ITA acts as a statutory sweep rule requiring a taxpayer to include the assistance directly in computing income from a business or property. Specifically, paragraph 12(1)(x) captures any inducement or assistance received in the year from a public authority where the amount can reasonably be considered to have been received as a reimbursement, contribution, allowance, or as assistance, whether as a grant, subsidy, forgivable loan, deduction from tax, allowance, or any other form of assistance. Finally, the statutory architecture provides no upfront exemption for repayable assistance upon receipt; instead, tax relief is deferred to the back end when actual repayment occurs in a future taxation year. When a taxpayer repays government assistance pursuant to a legal obligation, subparagraph 20(1)(hh)(i) permits an income deduction for amounts previously included under paragraph 12(1)(x), paragraph 37(1)(c) adds the repaid amount back to the subsection 37(1) pool, and paragraph (e.1) of the definition of "investment tax credit" in subsection 127(9), together with subsections 127(10.1) and (10.7) (claimed via Line 560 of Form T661), restores ITC eligibility strictly in the taxation year of repayment.
The Courts' Final Holding and Subsequent Legislative Aftermath

At the Tax Court of Canada (2021 TCC 57), by judgment rendered September 14, 2021 and amended November 8, 2021, Justice Sylvain Ouimet dismissed CAE's appeal, ruling at paragraphs 137 and 143 that because the SADI Agreement was not an ordinary commercial agreement—its implicit rate of return being significantly lower than the market rate for a comparable loan—the $57,084,395 and $59,148,888 contributed for 2012 and 2013 constituted "government assistance" under subsections 127(9) and 127(18) of the ITA; having so concluded, he did not examine the alternative question under subparagraphs 12(1)(x)(iii) and (iv) (paragraph 144).

In its March 14, 2022 Factum (Mémoire des faits et du droit de l'appelante) to the Federal Court of Appeal in Docket A-264-21, CAE argued that the trial judge had committed an extricable error of law reviewable on a standard of correctness, and maintained that neither the unconditionally repayable Capital nor the interest rate Differential constituted government assistance: the Capital because it was fully and unconditionally repayable, and the Differential because, although an advantage to CAE, it was not an amount "received" as required by paragraph 37(1)(d), subsection 127(18) and subparagraphs 12(1)(x)(iv) and (v). At the October 19, 2022 hearing, as recorded at paragraph [2] of the FCA's reasons, CAE admitted that the agreement was in the nature of government assistance but argued that a distinction nevertheless had to be made between the capital loan and the interest rate differential.

On October 19, 2022, the Federal Court of Appeal (Boivin, de Montigny, and Locke JJ.A.) delivered a unanimous judgment from the bench in Montreal (2022 FCA 178), dismissing CAE's appeal with costs. Writing for the Court, Justice Boivin held that Justice Ouimet properly directed himself under the binding jurisprudential trilogy of Canada v. Consumers' Gas Co., [1987] 2 F.C. 60 (FCA), Canada v. CCLC Technologies Inc., [1996] F.C.J. No. 1226 (QL) (FCA), and Immunovaccine Technologies Inc. v. Canada, 2014 FCA 196, and committed no palpable and overriding error of fact or mixed fact and law under the standard of Housen v. Nikolaisen, 2002 SCC 33. The Federal Court of Appeal expressly rejected CAE's bifurcation argument, holding that neither Canadian case law nor the text of the ITA supports separating the principal of a non-commercial government loan from its interest subsidy.

On May 25, 2023, the Supreme Court of Canada dismissed CAE's application for leave to appeal, cementing 2022 FCA 178 as the definitive judicial interpretation of the unamended statute. However, because the ruling meant that accessing federal low-interest innovation or clean-energy loans would cannibalize SR&ED and green ITCs while triggering immediate income tax on borrowed principal, the Joint Committee on Taxation of the Canadian Bar Association and CPA Canada petitioned the Department of Finance for urgent statutory intervention in August 2023. In the Fall Economic Statement released on November 21, 2023, the federal government announced proposed legislative amendments clarifying that a bona fide loan (including a concessional low- or zero-interest loan) with reasonable repayment terms from a public authority is generally excluded from "government assistance"; as enacted by Bill C-69 (Budget Implementation Act, 2024, No. 1, royal assent June 20, 2024), the relieving rule applies retroactively to loans made after 2019. Nevertheless, because those amendments did not retroactively cure CAE's assessed years—and because any public funding arrangement that fails the strict new statutory criteria for a bona fide loan with "reasonable repayment terms" remains governed by the CAE Inc. doctrine—the analytical framework of 2022 FCA 178 remains essential for Canadian tax practitioners.
2. Core Legal & Evidentiary Failures

A nuanced reading of the Tax Court judgment (2021 TCC 57), CAE's March 2022 Appellate Factum (Mémoire des faits et du droit de l'appelante), and the Federal Court of Appeal's decision (2022 FCA 178) reveals that CAE's disqualification did not stem from any deficiency in its underlying engineering or scientific documentation. Unlike typical SR&ED litigation where the CRA challenges whether the taxpayer faced "technological uncertainty" or executed a systematic investigation, in CAE Inc. both parties accepted that Project Falcon constituted valid SR&ED. Instead, the disallowance of CAE's SR&ED ITCs and the resulting income inclusion arose from four fatal legal, contractual, financial, and evidentiary failures under the ITA's funded-research and government assistance provisions.
Failure 1: Contractual Inability to Satisfy the "Ordinary Commercial Terms" Test

Under Canadian appellate jurisprudence anchored in Consumers' Gas, CCLC Technologies, and Immunovaccine, a payment or advance from a public authority escapes characterization as "government assistance" under subsection 127(9) and subparagraph 12(1)(x)(iv) only if it is made in the exact same manner as a public authority or private party conducting ordinary commercial business—that is, where the state acts solely to advance its own commercial or financial return rather than to subsidize or promote the business interests of the taxpayer. At trial before the Tax Court, CAE's primary contractual failure was its inability to demonstrate that the SADI Agreement possessed the attributes of an ordinary commercial loan.

Justice Ouimet examined the terms of the March 30, 2009 SADI Agreement (as amended in March 2010, February 2011, January 2012 and March 2013) and, as the Federal Court of Appeal summarized at paragraph [3] of its reasons, held that it was not an ordinary commercial agreement in view of its terms and, more specifically, its implicit rate of return. Foremost among these was the below-market concessional interest rate: the effective interest rate charged by Industry Canada under the SADI Agreement was approximately 2.5%, which the trial judge found significantly lower than the market rate of return for a comparable loan and therefore contrary to the business interests of a private lender; CAE's own financial statements valued the Differential at $122,975,399, being the difference between interest at the SADI rate ($87,500,000) and at the market rate for a comparable loan ($210,475,399). Despite committing up to $250,000,000 in funding, calculated at 35% of eligible Project Falcon expenditures over 2009–2014, the Department of Industry's return was limited to that implicit ~2.5% yield. Furthermore, the SADI Agreement granted an extended repayment moratorium that permitted CAE to draw down funds across a five-year SR&ED execution phase without any principal repayment obligations until after the research phase concluded. Finally, the SADI Agreement also imposed public-policy obligations on CAE, including an undertaking to manufacture exclusively in Canada all products that may result from Project Falcon, periodic progress and program-results reporting to the Department of Industry, restrictions on transferring title or rights in Project Falcon intellectual property, and an obligation to establish a collaboration plan with accredited Canadian post-secondary institutions and allocate to them at least 1.0% of total eligible project costs. Because the implicit rate of return was such that a private lender would not have made the loan on those terms, the trial judge held that the SADI Agreement failed the "ordinary commercial agreement" threshold and characterized the Capital received under it as government assistance.
Failure 2: Legal Failure of the "Bifurcation" Theory in the March 2022 Factum

In its March 14, 2022 Factum to the Federal Court of Appeal, CAE's counsel framed the appeal as raising an extricable error of law in the interpretation of "government assistance," reviewable on a standard of correctness under Vavilov and Housen v. Nikolaisen. As recorded in paragraph [2] of 2022 FCA 178, CAE formally conceded before the FCA that the SADI Agreement was in the nature of government assistance, but argued that Justice Ouimet erred in law by failing to bifurcate the transaction into two distinct legal components: the unconditionally repayable capital loan principal on one hand, and the interest rate differential (the economic value of the below-market interest rate) on the other.

In its Factum (specifically framing the issue at paragraph 32 of its written submissions), CAE argued that the statutory connectives in the ITA—an amount the taxpayer "has received, is entitled to receive or can reasonably be expected to receive" under paragraph 37(1)(d) and subsection 127(18), and an amount received "as" (à titre de) government assistance under subparagraph 12(1)(x)(iv)—require the Court to identify a specific "amount" or "sum" (as defined in subsection 248(1)) actually received that represents government assistance, rather than an economic benefit. CAE contended that because it was subject to an absolute, unconditional, full-recourse legal obligation to repay every dollar of principal advanced under the SADI Agreement, the principal itself did not enrich CAE and could not legally constitute "assistance". According to CAE's Factum, the interest rate Differential, although an advantage to CAE, was not an amount "received" and therefore could not produce any reducing effects, and the respondent's approach was incongruous because any single non-market term could taint an entire unconditionally repayable loan and treat it like a non-repayable grant.

The Federal Court of Appeal's rejection of this bifurcation theory highlights a critical doctrinal pitfall in Canadian tax law. The FCA held that it could find no support in either the case law (Consumers' Gas, CCLC Technologies, Immunovaccine) or the legislation for the distinction CAE proposed between the capital loan and the interest rate differential. As applied by the Tax Court and upheld on appeal, the inquiry is binary and holistic: because the financing instrument as a whole was found not to be an ordinary commercial agreement, the entire contribution amounts received or receivable under it ($57,084,395 for 2012 and $59,148,888 for 2013) were characterized as government assistance under subsection 127(9). Moreover, the back-end statutory relief mechanisms described in CAE's own Factum—paragraph 37(1)(c), paragraph (e.1) of the definition of "investment tax credit" in subsection 127(9) with subsections 127(10.1) and (10.7), and subparagraph 20(1)(hh)(i)—operate only when the assistance is actually repaid, so that repayable government assistance is captured in full upon receipt and relieved strictly upon repayment.
Failure 3: Evidentiary Disconnect Between Financial Accounting Treatment and Statutory Tax Law

A major technical and evidentiary trap revealed by CAE Inc. is the divergence between financial accounting characterization of concessional loans and the statutory provisions of the ITA. In corporate financial reporting, when a public corporation like CAE receives a below-market government loan, economic measurement principles separate the discounted present value of the debt liability (measured using a prevailing commercial market interest rate) from the benefit of the below-market interest rate.

CAE's appellate bifurcation thesis relied heavily on this economic distinction between loan principal and interest rate differential. However, in Canadian tax litigation, economic or accounting bifurcation does not override clear statutory definitions unless the statute expressly incorporates it. On the contrary, the quantification of the Differential—$122,975,399, being the difference between interest at the SADI rate ($87,500,000) and at the market rate for a comparable loan ($210,475,399), which CAE itself presented as a "government benefit" in its GAAP financial statements—formed part of the evidentiary record on which the Tax Court found that the SADI loan was concessional and not granted on ordinary commercial terms. Once that factual threshold was crossed, the Tax Court declined any economic bifurcation and treated 100% of the contributions received or receivable as "government assistance" under subsections 127(9) and 127(18).
Failure 4: Direct Linkage of Funding Draws to SR&ED Expenditure Claims Without Structural Segregation

Finally, from a project governance and documentation standpoint, the SADI Agreement linked Industry Canada's cash disbursements directly to a reimbursement of CAE's eligible SR&ED costs incurred on Project Falcon during each claim period. Because the drawdowns under the SADI Agreement were contractually tethered to the exact same Project Falcon costs claimed on Form T661, the advances were indisputably received "in respect of" (à l'égard de) SR&ED within the meaning of paragraph 37(1)(d) and subsection 127(18). Furthermore, because the SADI amount received or receivable in 2012 ($55,810,430) exceeded CAE's SR&ED expenditures for that year ($41,003,491), the Minister included the $14,806,939 excess in CAE's 2012 income under subparagraphs 12(1)(x)(iv) and (v); the Tax Court, having decided the appeal under subsections 127(9) and 127(18), did not examine the paragraph 12(1)(x) question.
3. Comparative Summary Table

The following table maps each statutory and jurisprudential requirement examined in CAE Inc. v. The Queen (2021 TCC 57) and CAE Inc. v. His Majesty the King (2022 FCA 178) against the taxpayer's specific legal or evidentiary failure and the governing judicial standard of proof applied by the Canadian courts.

cells: Subsection 127(9) ITA ("government assistance" / aide gouvernementale)

Assistance from a government, municipality, or public authority whether as a grant, subsidy, forgivable loan, tax deduction, investment allowance, or "any other form of assistance" reduces qualified SR&ED expenditures.
CAE assumed that an unconditionally repayable, non-forgivable, full-recourse loan could not constitute "any other form of assistance" because it created an absolute liability to repay principal.

Statutory Interpretation & Balance of Probabilities: Following CCLC Technologies and Immunovaccine, the phrase "any other form of assistance" is broad enough to capture the full principal of an unconditionally repayable loan if its terms are non-commercial.
The "Ordinary Commercial Terms" Test (Consumers' Gas, CCLC Technologies, Immunovaccine)

Public funding escapes characterization as "government assistance" only if advanced under ordinary commercial terms where the state acts as a commercial lender seeking a market financial return rather than promoting public policy or subsidizing the taxpayer.

The SADI Agreement carried an implicit return of ~2.5% (significantly below the market rate for a comparable loan, a Differential of $122,975,399), provided contributions over 2009–2014 with repayments beginning only in 2015, and imposed public-policy obligations (Canadian manufacturing, reporting, IP-transfer restrictions, 1.0% post-secondary allocation).

Evidentiary Benchmark Comparison: The taxpayer bears the burden of demolishing the Minister's assumptions by proving with market evidence that the interest rate, security, amortization, and covenants match arm's-length commercial credit facilities.
Transaction Bifurcation Doctrine (CAE's March 2022 FCA Factum, Docket A-264-21)

CAE argued in its FCA Factum that only an "amount" actually "received" can trigger the reductions in s. 37(1)(d), s. 127(18) and s. 12(1)(x)(iv); that the unconditionally repayable Capital is not government assistance; and that the interest rate Differential, though an advantage, is not an amount received.

At the hearing, CAE admitted that the agreement was in the nature of government assistance (FCA, para. [2]) but argued for a distinction between the capital loan and the interest rate differential; the FCA found no support for that distinction in the case law or the legislation.

Correctness (Law) & Palpable and Overriding Error (Mixed Fact/Law - Housen v. Nikolaisen): The FCA held that neither the ITA nor Canadian jurisprudence supports bifurcating a concessional loan; 100% of the principal is tainted as assistance.
Paragraph 37(1)(d) & Subsection 127(18) ITA (SR&ED Pool & ITC Reduction)

Any government assistance received, entitled to be received, or reasonably expected to be received "in respect of" SR&ED at the tax filing deadline reduces the s. 37(1) expenditure pool and s. 127(9) qualified expenditures for ITCs.
The SADI Agreement contractually tied each cash disbursement to eligible Project Falcon SR&ED expenditures, establishing a direct nexus ("in respect of" SR&ED).

Broad Nexus Standard ("In Respect Of"): Any funding agreement whose drawdowns are calculated by reference to, or conditioned upon incurring, SR&ED expenditures is conclusively received "in respect of" SR&ED.
Subparagraph 12(1)(x)(iv) ITA (Inclusion of Assistance in Business Income)

Any amount received in the year from a public authority "as" a contribution or any other form of assistance in the course of earning business income must be included in taxable income to the extent it does not reduce deductible SR&ED pools.

Because the SADI amount received or receivable in 2012 ($55,810,430) exceeded CAE's 2012 SR&ED expenditures ($41,003,491), the Minister added the $14,806,939 excess to CAE's 2012 business income under s. 12(1)(x)(iv) and (v).

Strict Statutory Application: The Minister applied the parallel wording of s. 12(1)(x)(iv) and (v) to include the unapplied excess in income upon receipt; having found government assistance under s. 127(9) and (18), the Tax Court did not examine the s. 12(1)(x) question (TCC Reasons, para. 144).
Form T661 Line 560 & Subsection 127(9) ITA (Back-End Repayment Relief)

Tax relief for repayable government assistance is unavailable upon loan origination; it is deferred until the taxation year in which the taxpayer actually repays the assistance pursuant to a legal obligation.

CAE sought upfront exclusion of the repayable loan principal in the years of receipt (2012 and 2013) rather than claiming back-end ITC restorations at Line 560 of Form T661 in future years as principal repayments were made.

Statutory Timing Rule: The existence of back-end repayment mechanisms confirms that Parliament intended repayable non-commercial loans to reduce ITCs upon receipt and generate tax relief strictly on a cash-repaid basis.

body.text: 4. Two Applied Remedial Case Studies

Following the Supreme Court of Canada's refusal to grant leave to appeal in CAE Inc. (May 25, 2023), the Department of Finance's announcement of a carve-out in the November 21, 2023 Fall Economic Statement, and its enactment by Bill C-69 (royal assent June 20, 2024) for loans made after 2019, Canadian R&D-intensive corporations face a complex compliance landscape. First, public funding agreements that include royalty-based repayments, revenue-sharing contingencies, conditional forgiveness, or indeterminate repayment schedules fail the statutory safe harbour for bona fide loans with "reasonable repayment terms" and remain fully exposed to the CAE Inc. total-principal clawback. Second, taxpayers with innovation loans made before 2020 or hybrid public-private debt facilities face aggressive CRA audit enforcement applying 2022 FCA 178.

The following two applied industry case studies demonstrate step-by-step how Canadian corporations can restructure their project governance, contract terms, technical documentation, and financial tracking to overcome the judicial traps identified in CAE Inc. and preserve full statutory SR&ED and Clean Economy ITC eligibility.
Case Study 1: Aerospace & Autonomous Avionics Developer Navigating Federal Innovation Contributions
Scenario and Legal Pitfall

AeroSim Dynamics Corp. ("AeroSim"), an aerospace manufacturer based in Montreal, Quebec, is executing a four-year, $40 million research program ("Project Horizon") to develop fault-tolerant quantum-inertial navigation algorithms and fly-by-wire actuator architectures for next-generation regional aircraft. AeroSim applies to Innovation, Science and Economic Development Canada ("ISED", the successor to Industry Canada) under a federal aerospace innovation program for $15 million in public financing.

ISED's initial draft Master Contribution Agreement ("MCA") proposes an interest-free advance of $15 million calculated as a 37.5% reimbursement of AeroSim's eligible SR&ED salaries, subcontractor fees, and materials incurred on Project Horizon. Crucially, the draft MCA stipulates that repayment is deferred for six years after project completion and that annual repayments are contingent upon AeroSim achieving benchmark gross revenues from commercializing the resulting avionics suite, with any unpaid balance forgiven after Year 15.

Under CAE Inc. v. His Majesty the King (2022 FCA 178) and Immunovaccine (2014 FCA 196)—as well as the concessional loan rules enacted in June 2024 for loans made after 2019—this draft MCA creates a severe tax exposure. Because repayment is conditionally tied to commercialization revenue and subject to potential forgiveness after Year 15, the facility does not qualify as a bona fide loan with reasonable repayment terms. Furthermore, because the advance is interest-free, unsecured, and calculated as a percentage reimbursement of Project Horizon's SR&ED costs, the CRA will classify 100% of the $15 million principal as "government assistance" under subsection 127(9). This will wipe out $15 million of AeroSim's qualified SR&ED expenditure pool under paragraph 37(1)(d) and subsection 127(18), eliminate millions of dollars in federal SR&ED ITCs, and trigger an immediate paragraph 12(1)(x) income inclusion for any excess loan principal.
Step-by-Step Remedial Restructuring Plan
Step 1: Contractual Restructuring of Debt Terms and Structural Severance

To prevent the $15 million principal from being characterized as "government assistance" under subsection 127(9) and subparagraph 12(1)(x)(iv), AeroSim's tax counsel must renegotiate the ISED MCA prior to execution. The primary remedial action is to bring the debt instrument squarely within the statutory safe harbour for bona fide concessional loans from public authorities, enacted in June 2024 for loans made after 2019. AeroSim must eliminate all forgiveness and revenue-contingent repayment clauses from the agreement, replacing them with an unconditional, full-recourse covenant to repay 100% of the borrowed principal on a fixed, deterministic amortization schedule. By specifying a fixed maturity date and scheduled principal instalments that do not depend on project revenues or royalties, the loan satisfies the statutory requirement of a bona fide loan with reasonable repayment terms, thereby exempting the entire principal even if the interest rate is zero or below market.

If ISED insists on retaining conditional or royalty-linked repayment features for a portion of the funding package, AeroSim must avoid the ex post facto bifurcation error rejected by the Federal Court of Appeal in CAE Inc. by executing two legally separate contracts from inception. Under this dual-contract architecture, Facility 1 ($11 million) is executed as a standalone, unconditionally repayable, fixed-schedule loan dedicated to eligible SR&ED activities, qualifying for exclusion from government assistance as a bona fide loan with reasonable repayment terms. Simultaneously, Facility 2 ($4 million) is executed as a separate conditional contribution agreement whose Schedule of Eligible Costs explicitly restricts reimbursements exclusively to post-SR&ED commercial tooling, marketing, certification, and non-SR&ED facility expansion. Because Facility 2 is contractually prohibited from reimbursing SR&ED expenditures, it is never received "in respect of" SR&ED under paragraph 37(1)(d) or subsection 127(18), completely insulating AeroSim's Form T661 SR&ED ITC pools from clawback.
Step 2: Project Governance & Cost-Center Ring-Fencing

To withstand a CRA financial and technical audit, AeroSim must establish a strict internal governance protocol before incurring Project Horizon expenditures. AeroSim's enterprise resource planning (ERP) system must be configured into segregated General Ledger (GL) project codes that enforce a rigid wall between eligible experimental development and routine commercial engineering. Specifically, GL Series 100 must capture pure SR&ED work packages—comprising engineering salaries, experimental prototype materials, and eligible Canadian SR&ED subcontractors directly addressing areas of technological uncertainty—and may only draw funds from the unconditional Facility 1 loan or internal corporate working capital. Conversely, GL Series 200 must capture non-SR&ED commercialization, Transport Canada regulatory certification testing, production readiness, and commercial flight-deck assembly, serving as the sole cost repository eligible for reimbursement under the conditional Facility 2 agreement. A monthly R&D Tax and Treasury Review Committee comprising the Vice President of Engineering, Corporate Controller, and Tax Director must audit every claim submitted to ISED to certify that no conditional government funds are ever mapped against GL Series 100 cost centers.
Step 3: Technical Documentation & Experimentation Tracking

While CAE Inc. focused on financial assistance, the CRA routinely audits the technical boundary between eligible SR&ED and routine aerospace development when reviewing government-funded claims to verify which costs the public funding actually reimbursed. AeroSim must implement contemporaneous technical tracking that proves the exact boundary between GL Series 100 and GL Series 200. For each work package in GL Series 100, lead avionics systems engineers must maintain contemporaneous version-control and test repositories documenting the system-level technological baseline and why existing flight control architectures fail to resolve sensor drift in areas of technological uncertainty. These records must chronologically track formulated hypotheses, hardware-in-the-loop simulation logs, failure analysis metrics, and iterative algorithmic modifications. Crucially, the technical narratives must record the exact milestone date when technological uncertainty is resolved, immediately shifting all subsequent engineering hours for environmental stress testing and aviation software certification into GL Series 200, where conditional government funding can be absorbed without reducing SR&ED ITCs.
Step 4: Financial Reporting Reconciliation and Form T661 Execution

To prevent the evidentiary trap that ensnared CAE—where financial statement disclosures measuring the below-market interest benefit were used by the Crown to establish a non-commercial subsidy—AeroSim must implement a specialized tax-to-accounting reconciliation protocol. When AeroSim's external auditors discount the low-interest ISED loan on the audited financial statements to recognize a notional interest benefit, the Tax Director must prepare a formal T2 Schedule 1 reconciliation memorandum. This memorandum eliminates the accounting grant amortization from net income for tax purposes and documents how Facility 1 satisfies every statutory condition of a bona fide loan with reasonable repayment terms. Furthermore, if AeroSim holds any legacy pre-2020 SADI or SIF advances that were previously assessed as government assistance under CAE Inc., the tax team must track every dollar of principal repaid during the current taxation year and claim the restoration of qualified SR&ED expenditures on Line 560 of Form T661 to regenerate the previously lost SR&ED ITCs.
Case Study 2: Clean-Tech Hydrogen & Carbon Capture Enterprise Structuring Public Authority Financing Alongside SR&ED and Clean Economy ITCs
Scenario and Legal Pitfall

TerraCathode Clean Energy Inc. ("TerraCathode"), a Canadian industrial clean-technology corporation, is developing a novel solid-oxide electrolysis cell ("SOEC") stack integrated with a waste-biomass synthesis gas reformer ("Project Verde"). Project Verde comprises two concurrent engineering and capital streams during the 2026–2028 taxation years. The first stream involves $25 million in experimental stack and catalyst development (the SR&ED Stream), investigating novel cathode formulations to prevent sulfur poisoning and thermal delamination during rapid load cycling, claimed for SR&ED ITCs under section 37 and subsection 127(9) of the ITA. The second stream involves $120 million in commercial-scale clean hydrogen electrolyzers and waste-biomass heat and electricity generating equipment (the Clean Economy ITC Stream), claimed for the Clean Hydrogen Investment Tax Credit ("CHITC") and Clean Technology Investment Tax Credit ("CTITC").

To finance Project Verde, TerraCathode negotiates a $50 million financing package from a federal public authority (such as the Canada Infrastructure Bank). The proposed term sheet offers a single $50 million hybrid credit facility at a 1.5% interest rate, under which $10 million of principal is automatically forgiven if TerraCathode achieves a verified carbon intensity ("CI") below a target threshold, while repayments on the remaining $40 million are deferred until Project Verde generates positive cash flow, with interest capitalized indefinitely if cash flows fall short.

As highlighted by Canadian tax counsel analyzing the interaction between CAE Inc. v. His Majesty the King (2022 FCA 178) and the Clean Economy ITCs, this hybrid term sheet creates a severe tax trap. Under the ITA, both SR&ED ITCs and the Clean Economy ITCs require the taxpayer to reduce eligible expenditures and capital cost by any "government assistance". Because the $50 million facility bundles a $10 million performance-forgivable tranche with an indeterminate, cash-flow-contingent repayment structure in a single unsegregated agreement, the entire $50 million principal fails the CAE Inc. commerciality test and fails the statutory exception for bona fide loans with reasonable repayment terms. Under the anti-bifurcation holding of 2022 FCA 178 (paragraph [4]), a court will refuse to separate the $40 million repayable tranche from the $10 million forgivable tranche. Consequently, the entire $50 million loan will be deemed "government assistance," slashing TerraCathode's SR&ED ITCs and Clean Economy ITCs while exposing any unapplied loan balance to immediate taxation under paragraph 12(1)(x).
Step-by-Step Remedial Restructuring Plan
Step 1: Contractual Unbundling and Legal Severance of Credit Facilities Prior to Execution

Because the Federal Court of Appeal in CAE Inc. held that a taxpayer cannot ask a court to retroactively bifurcate a single hybrid government financing agreement, TerraCathode must legally sever the $50 million package into two independent, standalone contracts with distinct legal obligations before signing. Contract 1 must be structured as a $40 million Senior Unconditional Term Loan Agreement drafted as a standalone, non-forgivable, full-recourse debt instrument at the 1.5% concessional interest rate. All cash-flow or earnings contingencies must be removed and replaced with a fixed 12-year amortization schedule featuring mandatory semi-annual principal and interest payments and an express "Entire Agreement" clause with zero cross-forgiveness links to any other instrument. Because Contract 1 is an independent bona fide loan with reasonable repayment terms from a public authority, 100% of the $40 million principal is statutorily excluded from "government assistance," allowing TerraCathode to stack the low-interest public loan with both SR&ED ITCs and Clean Economy ITCs without offset.

Concurrently, Contract 2 must isolate the $10 million carbon-intensity performance incentive into a separate Forgivable Loan Agreement. Because Contract 2 is a forgivable loan, it falls squarely within the definition of "government assistance" under subsection 127(9). To prevent this $10 million from eroding high-rate SR&ED or Clean Economy ITCs, Contract 2's "Use of Proceeds" covenant must explicitly allocate and restrict the $10 million strictly to non-creditable project expenditures—such as land acquisition, civil site grading, administrative buildings, and working capital—that are ineligible for both SR&ED ITCs (subsection 37(1)) and Clean Hydrogen or Clean Technology ITCs. By directing the forgivable assistance exclusively to non-ITC civil assets, TerraCathode preserves 100% of its SR&ED and Clean Economy ITC bases.
Step 2: Project Governance & Multi-Credit Boundary Controls

When a taxpayer claims both SR&ED ITCs and Clean Economy ITCs on an integrated industrial facility, the CRA audits not only government assistance but also the boundary between experimental prototypes and commercial capital property. TerraCathode must institute a formal Engineering and Tax Charter signed by the Chief Technology Officer and Vice President of Tax that segregates Project Verde into three isolated cost pools in the accounting ledger. Pool A (SR&ED Experimental Development — Form T661) must capture sub-scale SOEC test rigs and experimental catalyst batches destroyed during sulfur-tolerance testing, funded solely by internal equity and draws from Contract 1. Pool B (Eligible Clean Hydrogen and Clean Tech Property) must capture commercial-scale electrolyzers and waste-biomass heat and electricity generating equipment meeting the 11,000 BTU/kWh heat rate threshold, also funded solely by internal equity and Contract 1. Pool C (Non-Creditable Civil Infrastructure) must capture access roads, structural foundations, and administrative buildings, funded via a dedicated, segregated bank account holding the proceeds of Contract 2. Every disbursement from the Contract 2 bank account must be traced directly to Pool C vendor invoices, establishing an irrefutable audit trail proving that the forgivable assistance was never received "in respect of" SR&ED or eligible Clean Economy ITC property.
Step 3: Technical Documentation & Experimentation Tracking

To defend Pool A (SR&ED) and Pool B (Clean Economy ITCs) during a joint CRA audit, TerraCathode must maintain strictly separated technical compliance dossiers. For Pool A, chemical engineers must compile systematic investigation dossiers documenting the thermodynamic and metallurgical uncertainties of the cathode reformulation separately from commercial balance-of-plant engineering, preserving time-stamped laboratory notebooks, microscopy degradation logs, and parametric test matrices showing how specific hypotheses regarding thermal cycling delamination were tested. For Pool B, project engineers must maintain independent Natural Resources Canada ("NRCan") front-end engineering design carbon-intensity validation reports, verified operational CI compliance logs, heat-rate calculations confirming the 11,000 BTU/kWh threshold for waste-biomass equipment, and contemporaneous payroll records proving compliance with prevailing union wage and apprenticeship requirements under the Clean Economy ITC rules.
Step 4: Contemporaneous Financial & Tax Compliance Execution

Even when relying on the statutory exception for bona fide concessional loans, TerraCathode must assemble a contemporaneous "Loan Commerciality and Repayment Viability Defense File" at the time Contract 1 is executed. This defense file must include 12-year financial projections demonstrating that TerraCathode possesses the realistic financial capacity to service and repay 100% of the $40 million principal according to the fixed schedule, preempting any CRA audit assertion that the loan lacks reasonable repayment terms or operates as a disguised grant. Prior to filing its corporate T2 return, TerraCathode's tax advisors must cross-reference all tax schedules to ensure that the $10 million forgivable assistance under Contract 2 is applied to reduce the capital cost of Pool C non-ITC civil depreciable property (preventing an unapplied income inclusion under subparagraph 12(1)(x)(iv)), while Pool A (Form T661) and Pool B (Clean Economy ITC schedules) reflect zero government assistance reductions from Contract 1, securing 100% of TerraCathode's statutory R&D and clean-economy tax incentives.
